sections.text: हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम्।
If killed, thou shalt attain Heaven; if victorious, enjoy the kingdom of earth. Therefore arise, O Son of Kunti, and fight!
Look upon pleasure and pain, victory and defeat, with an equal eye. Make ready for the combat, and thou shalt commit no sin.
एषा तेऽभिहिता साङ्ख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां शृणु।
I have told thee the philosophy of Knowledge. Now listen and I will explain the philosophy of Action, by means of which, O Arjuna, thou shalt break through the bondage of all action.

We had been discussing Chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, Yoga of Knowledge. So far we have seen in the chapter that Bhagavan explained to Arjuna his situation from various perspectives -- not just one perspective saying, this is my idea, you should do this. He gave him various perspectives. The first was the spiritual perspective, from the highest point of view: the self is immutable, imperishable. So thats the highest perspective. Then it came down to the societys perspective.
And see, from a societys perspective, you as a Kshatriya have a duty to protect the society from evil. If you see that evil is occurring in the society, we rely on the Kshatriya just like we rely on our armies to protect ourselves. Our army cannot become pacifist at the last minute. From that perspective, this is the best opportunity you have to perform your duty. So from societys perspective, he gave his opinion that this is still what you should be looking at. Then came the individuals perspective.
There we have seen Bhagavan said, if you give up and run away from your duty, then you will incur sin. He has looked at the issue from various perspectives and came to the same conclusion that Arjuna should fight this war.
So in the process, Bhagavan also taught us the art of persuasion. If you want to persuade somebody who is bent upon doing something other than what we think is right for him, just giving your opinion -- look, you are doing something wrong -- is not going to work. The only way that works is when you give him a three-dimensional view of his situation from various perspectives. Look at it from various points of view, and then the person will be able to see it correctly. Then you will be able to persuade him. This can also be applicable to looking at any problem, any situation.
You come across a situation where you got a job in another town, thats best for you. From your professional perspective, well thats great. But if you take the decision just based on that, it may or may not be right. So you have to look at it from various perspectives. First you say, well from a professional perspective it seems like that job will give me more opportunity to go further in my career. Then you see it from familys perspective.
Will my family be comfortable relocating from this town to another? Will they be able to adjust as easily as they are adjusted here? Then lastly, you also have to see what the school district is like in that new town. Is it as good or better? And if you come to the same conclusion from all three perspectives, then relocation is a great idea. Take the job and move -- or you will find that you will end up commuting just like most of our friends do who work outside Richmond in Washington or other places.
So any problem or situation cannot be viewed from just one perspective. And you can come to right decision or you can convince someone. So this art of persuasion is to give somebody a three dimensional view of a situation and then come to the conclusion. In this case, Bhagavan came to the same conclusion from all perspectives. From a spiritual, from a societys perspective, from individual Arjuna must fight this war. What typically works best is when it comes to me and I can see from my own perspective that it is right.
So therefore Bhagavan put more stress on his individual situation. So we have seen that hes saying tathaha swadharma kirtim hitva papa vapsyasi. If you give up your duties, you will incur Papa. And this obviously is very dreaded word in Hindu society that you will incur papa. So that obviously worked probably more effectively. But you had the background of other two perspectives that this is right, this is the right thing to do from all perspectives.
So Bhagavan pursue that point of view a little further and says, bhayat ranat uparatam mansante tvam maharathaha isam chatvam bahumatah bhatva yasyasi lagavam. So all these great warriors who are gathered here on our side and on the other side, they have very high regards for you. Because of your valor and your prowess. They are unwillingly accepting your enemy, unwillingly accepting that you are one of the best warriors. It is not easy to confront you. You are the one who has achieved the pasupatastra from Lord Shiva himself.
Obviously theres a story that Arjunaya goes for tapas to please Lord Shiva. And in the end he ended up fighting with Lord Shiva himself. But Lord Shiva was so pleased that he revealed himself that I am not just the hunter which you are fighting, but I am Lord Shiva. Here is the Pashupadashtra. And as the Purana says, the Pasupatastra is like ultimate weapon. It can destroy the entire universe in no time.
So you are the one who has such a prowess that you can destroy everybody in no time if you really choose to. However, you cannot use any weapon irresponsibly. Just like our nuclear weapons. You may have capability but you may never use it. He said those people, they will then think that you ran away from this war because of fear. Even though that may not be reality but thats how you will be viewed by your peers and your enemies.
They will belittle you. Right now they have high respect for you, and they will say, I dont know what we were thinking. This guy turned out to be not really what we thought he was going to be. Its not something very comfortable for you if that happens.
So the next verse says: not only will you disappoint your friends and relatives and people who are relying on you, the society.
But there are ahitha people who are not your well wishers, you know, enemies who wish that you go away. He said they will be telling stories about your cowardice. All kinds of, you know, Bahun, vadish, shanti or vachevadas. Things which we cannot repeat on national tv. That kind of talk, they will be talking about you. So please think about it.
Ninantaha, tava, samaratyam. They will be cavilling at your prowess. That I think it was all big hype. It was all made up stories that he is such a great warrior. I dont think he had those qualities. And if thats happened, what is more painful than that?
Nobody will ever realize that you ran away because you thought that killing your cousins and your teachers is not a right thing to do. They will think its a fear of war, fear of defeat, which made you go away. So dont think this is going to be easy if you go away.
And then, in any deal which we make, you have to come up with a win-win situation. The only way a deal gets closed is when a client comes to me and thinks I can provide the most appropriate services, and I think this is the right project for me -- then only we sign a contract. If I dont think it is right, or he doesnt think it is right for him, nothing happens.
So you have to come up with a win-win situation where both parties will have a good outcome. Now in this case, if you are just looking at your own situation, any decision which I take out of the options available to me, I should feel comfortable that it will be an acceptable situation for me. So Bhagavan now uses that final trump card and says: if you die, you will go to the heros heaven. So there is a special section of heaven which is reserved for these great heroes who die on the battlefield.
Its like the GI Bill, these great privileges in heaven for the heroes who serve their country, serve the society, in the process they die. You can think about the health care workers who lost their lives in this battle against Corona. So here our scripture says they have a special Saxon in heaven to reward them for their valor and their courage. Hatova Prapsesi Swargam Jitwava Bakshishe Mahim. If you die, you go to the heaven for the heroes. If you win, you will lead the kingdom on this earth.
This is a no-brainer for you. There is no way that you can lose, one way or the other. Fight and die, or fight and win -- both ways you come out ahead. So there is nothing to think about. Here the only good decision is to fight the war. Therefore he says, Tasmat Utthishtka Yudhaya Krutan Nishayah.
Therefore O son of Kunti, get up with a resolve to fight this war. So this is like a conclusive statement from Bhagavan. In the beginning Arjuna asked him and said, give me which is shreyas for me. And we have come across the word shreyas and prayers before. That which is always good. It may not feel good, but it is good for me.
Preyas, on the other hand, feels good but is not good for me. And Arjuna, in no uncertain terms, asked Bhagavan: tell me what is good for me and I will do it. Now Bhagavan says Utthiste Kaunteya, get up with the resolve to fight this war. So that was the conclusive advice from Bhagavan. And then Bhagavan now introduces the concept of Karma Yoga. You have to act in this world and there will be consequences of your actions.
You are part of this world. This Sansar is not made up of homogeneous experiences. The experiences are varied -- some are conducive, some are not conducive. You will fight the war. Outcome is not guaranteed.
The experience will not be as you predict. It may be something different. But you have to treat whatever you face with an equal state of mind. You have to treat them alike no matter what the outcome is. Because you are enjoying the ride in this world. The next verse now introduces the idea of how to transform Karma into Karma Yoga.
Same action, changing the mental attitude becomes Karma yoga. It says Sukhdu KE samy krutva alabha jaya jayo Tathaya yujaswa na evam papam avapsyasi. We came back to the papa again. So in verse 33 he said that Tathaha swadharma kirtim chahitva papam awapsyasi. You will incur sin if you abandon your duty. Here he says Tatha yudhaya yujyashwa na evam papam avapshasi.
You will not incur any sin. But the condition is sukha dukkha samay krutva sukhyana dukkha. You should treat them alike. Its more like an observer. It does not mean that you react to Sukhanidukha in the same way but you treat them alike as an observer. Its like that to me.
One part of me says, I think I should have a cup of coffee. The one who is thinking about me having a cup of coffee -- thats the observer. See, that observer should be neutral. He should be treating anything which comes alike. Sukha and Dukkha operate at the mental level -- my experience. When I experience something, there will be a mental reaction: this is conducive or this is not conducive.
Then there is profit and loss -- that operates at the intellectual level. Am I making a profit by doing this, or am I losing something? Thats my intellect at work. I actually thought I was going to get this, but I didnt get that.
And therefore this is a loss or this is a profit. So thats at the intellectual level. Finally both Jaya and Ajaya victory or defeat is at the physical level. I tried to gain something, I did not gain it. I competed against several firms to get a project. Thats a real reality, the physical reality that I dont have that project anymore.

Verse 37 presents a win-win scenario: If killed, thou shalt attain Heaven; if victorious, enjoy the kingdom of earth. Therefore arise, O Son of Kunti, and fight! Either outcome is favorable when one acts from duty with the right attitude. This removes the paralysis of what if I fail? - both success and failure have their rewards when the action itself is righteous.
Verse 38 introduces the transformative attitude of Karma Yoga: Look upon pleasure and pain, victory and defeat, with an equal eye. Make ready for the combat, and thou shalt commit no sin. This equanimity (Samatva) is the key that transforms ordinary action into yoga. And verse 39 transitions to the practical teaching: I have told thee the philosophy of Knowledge. Now listen and I will explain the philosophy of Action, by means of which... thou shalt break through the bondage of all action.
Practice this today by choosing one challenging task and approaching it with equanimity. Before beginning, consciously decide: I will give my best effort, and I will accept whatever outcome arises with equal composure. Notice the difference this makes - without attachment to results, you can focus fully on the action itself, making you more effective. At the days end, reflect: Did viewing success and failure equally allow you to act more freely? Did releasing outcome-attachment reduce your stress and increase your engagement? This is the beginning of Karma Yoga in daily life.
